articles.title: 'Why is this a special case?': Judge named accused in son’s fatal Mercedes crash gets anticipatory bail
articles.summary: KOCHI: The Kerala high court on Thursday granted anticipatory bail to an additional sessions judge whose minor son was allegedly involved in a car crash
articles.body: KOCHI: The Kerala high court on Thursday granted anticipatory bail to an additional sessions judge whose minor son was allegedly involved in a car crash that killed a scooterist on October 25.Justice Kauser Edappagath granted the relief after observing that there was nothing to suggest that the judicial officer would not cooperate with the ongoing investigation.The court questioned the need to arrest the judge, noting that his house had already been searched and items seized by investigators."You have searched his house seized everything. This is something affecting the liberty of a person, whether District Judge or anyone. You have no case that he has not cooperated," the court observed, as quoted by website Bar and Bench.It also questioned the state's insistence on custodial interrogation, even while considering the allegations against the judge to be true at this stage."Why is this a special case? A 16-page objection? This is an unfortunate case no doubt… Let's assume that all your allegations are true at this stage and the offence is prima facie attracted, including Section 105 BNS. Even then, why do you want to arrest him? Why do you want his custody?" Justice Edappagath asked the state's counsel, as quoted by Bar and Bench.The judge further questioned whether the judicial officer would refuse to cooperate with investigators."As a responsible officer of this court, do you think that a District Judge will not cooperate? The fact that you oppose the bail application shows that you want his arrest. Why is an arrest required? You mean to say that he will speak the truth only under custodial interrogation? It is very unfortunate to hear it from a lawyer," the court said, as quoted by Bar and Bench.What happened in the accident?The case relates to an accident in the early hours of October 25, when a 54-year-old man died after his two-wheeler was hit by a Mercedes-Benz car allegedly driven by the judge's minor son.The collision occurred near Cheranelloor between 2am and 3am, police said.A case was registered under Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deals with causing death by negligence.The minor was subsequently released on bail in accordance with the provisions of the Juvenile Justice Act, police said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news. articles.title: 45-year-old woman changing bedsheet plunges 15 feet into hidden Scindia-era chamber as floor caves in at historic house in Madhya Pradesh’s Bhind
articles.summary: BHOPAL: A 45-year-old woman fell nearly 15 feet into an underground pit, taking her bed down with her, when the floor of a room collapsed at a historic
articles.body: BHOPAL: A 45-year-old woman fell nearly 15 feet into an underground pit, taking her bed down with her, when the floor of a room collapsed at a historic house in Bhind on Wednesday night.The house, once a Scindia-era administrative court, sits atop an old chamber that was used to store grain collected as tax. She was changing the bedsheet when the ground gave way, said sources.The incident occurred at approximately 9:15 pm at a residence in Girls School Wali Gali. Family members and neighbours rescued her by lowering a ladder into the pit. She was admitted to hospital with injuries, and her condition is reported to be stable.According to the family, the premises functioned as a local administrative court during the Scindia State period and was used for revenue collection and administrative work in the surrounding areas. Grain collected as tax was stored in an underground structure locally known as a “galla khanti.” The cavity that opened on Wednesday is believed to be part of this original structure.The family said their great-grandfather, Pandit Madan Mohan Mishra, served as an honorary magistrate under the Scindia State and was also entrusted with duties related to the Van Khandeshwar Mahadev temple, say locals.The house was reconstructed in the 80s, and the family says the pit was sealed at that time. They suspect that years of water seepage gradually washed away the soil inside the abandoned structure, leaving a hollow beneath the floor that eventually gave way under pressure. Water was found at the bottom of the pit.Most household members were attending an invitation when the accident occurred and returned to find the woman trapped inside. The exact cause of the collapse and the condition of the underground structure have yet to be established.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhopal | Silver Rate in Bhopal | Bank Holidays in Bhopal | Public Holidays in Bhopal | Petrol Price in Bhopal | Diesel Price in Bhopal | CNG Price in Bhopal | LPG Price in BhopalStay updated with the latest Bhopal news. articles.title: Jeff Bezos' ex-wife MacKenzie Scott who sold half of her Amazon stake,  gave $30 million to a nonprofit community loan fund in Silicon Valley in 2024, a year later it shared 10-year plan to transform Bay Area's ...
articles.summary: A year after Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife MacKenzie Scott gave $30 million to a Silicon Valley-based nonprofit community loan fund Housing Trust Silicon Valley has
articles.body: A year after Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife MacKenzie Scott gave $30 million to a Silicon Valley-based nonprofit community loan fund Housing Trust Silicon Valley has unveiled a 10-year strategy aimed at turning the one-time gift into lasting housing solutions across the Bay Area. The organisation says the funding will help expand affordable housing initiatives, support first-time homebuyers, strengthen policy advocacy efforts and back innovative housing projects over the next decade. a San Jose-based community loan fund, announced on September 30, 2025, a 10-year plan for turning the unrestricted gift from Scott’s Yield Giving fund into long-term housing solutions across the Bay Area.From MacKenzie Scott’s surprise donation to long-term strategyHousing Trust announced the donation on October 2, 2024. CEO Noni Ramos called it “the largest from an individual in our history” and said it came as a surprise. The gift was unrestricted, which means the nonprofit can decide how to use it, and it was meant to help the organisation expand its work across the 14-county greater Bay Area. At the time, early ideas for the money included seeding a new capital raise for its loan fund, expanding existing programmes and launching new initiatives to deepen partnerships and increase equity and affordability in housing.The release highlighted two recent projects as examples of its work. At Meridian Apartments in Sunnyvale, Housing Trust provided a $2 million predevelopment loan, in partnership with Related California, to help create 90 affordable homes for families. In San Rafael, it supported Eden Housing with a $4 million loan for Vivalon, a 66-unit development for older adults that pairs affordable homes with supportive services.The 10-year planThe plan, developed with input from staff, the board and community stakeholders, has five major initiatives:* Lending capital and new products: Expanding the core revolving loan fund and piloting new tools to meet developers’ changing needs. More details were due at the organisation’s Investor Briefing on October 15.* Homeownership expansion: Beginning in 2026, extending first-time homebuyer programmes to reach more households across a wider area.* Policy and partnerships: Hiring new staff to strengthen advocacy and collaboration across sectors that could unlock more resources and affordable housing.* Impact measurement and management: Launching a framework in early 2026 to better track, evaluate and communicate results.* Innovation investments: Supporting mission-driven housing innovations that can reduce costs, shorten development timelines and increase affordability.Noni Ramos CEO of Housing Trust said the gift allows the organisation to take bold steps and carries both the responsibility and the freedom to scale what works, take calculated risks on new ideas and widen its reach. Board Chair Lisa Gutierrez, a senior vice president at U.S. Bank, said the plan is not about one-time dollars but about building momentum that compounds. By putting the funds to work strategically, she said, Housing Trust can attract new partners, expand homeownership and make loans to create and preserve rental housing in ways it could not before, while also strengthening the organisation itself.Building on 25 years of housing investmentThe announcement comes as Housing Trust Silicon Valley marks its 25th anniversary. Since its founding in 2000, the community development financial institution says it has invested more than $690 million, helped create over 28,700 affordable housing opportunities and supported more than 53,800 residents in finding homes they can afford. The organisation says its work has also leveraged nearly $9 billion in additional public and private capital.Board Chair Lisa Gutierrez said the goal is to use the donation strategically to attract new partners, expand homeownership opportunities and support loans for creating and preserving affordable rental housing, while strengthening the organisation's long-term capacity.The nonprofit said the decade-long strategy is designed to ensure that MacKenzie Scott's donation continues generating impact long after the original gift was received, helping create more affordable and stable housing opportunities across the Bay Area.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2014, Rory McIlroy committed £1 million to help establish Daisy Lodge, a support centre for children with cancer; by its 10th anniversary, the centre had provided more than 4,000 breaks to families.
articles.summary: Rory McIlroy loves to win. The Northern Irish golfer has four major titles, and he has never pretended otherwise.
articles.body: Rory McIlroy loves to win. The Northern Irish golfer has four major titles, and he has never pretended otherwise. But his idea of winning goes beyond the golf course. For McIlroy, success also means making a difference in the lives of others. That’s exactly why he donated £1 million to help establish Daisy Lodge, a therapeutic short-break centre in Newcastle, County Down, for children with cancer and their families. The centre, which started as a place of support for families facing difficult times, has now grown into something much bigger. Ten years after opening, Daisy Lodge had provided more than 4,000 therapeutic short breaks, helping families spend time together away from the demands of hospital appointments and cancer treatment.Daisy LodgePeople go on holidays to picturesque places. But Daisy Lodge, set against the Mourne Mountains in Newcastle, County Down, was built for a different purpose. It was created for the hardest weeks a family can face. The therapeutic short-break centre has spent a decade giving families a quiet place to rest, talk and be together.The Cancer Fund for Children opened the lodge in 2014. What’s unique about the centre? It’s not a hospital. Families come here for a short break. The centre arranges meals and organises workshops, while therapies are also part of every stay. But nobody is taking a blood test in the lounge. In the ten years since its opening, the charity says more than 4,000 families have come for a short break. These include parents with a child undergoing treatment, parents who have just received a diagnosis and families grieving the loss of a child.Rory McIlroy commits £1 millionRory McIlroy committed £1 million from his foundation to support the work. In 2014, during the centre’s development, he said the model should be replicated. “I definitely think it is a project I would like to see replicated and I think can be replicated. I don't think there is any reason why we should stop here,” he said, as reported by ITV.McIlroy’s name, attached to the centre, brings the work to the attention of people who might never have come across it otherwise. And the golfer says he is touched to be part of the vision. "It is about giving back and being able to help others."What the support means for the familiesIn 2025, the centre supported 962 individual families and received 293 new family referrals, according to its year-end report. “521 families availed of a short break at Daisy Lodge Newcastle,” Peter O’Brien, the chairperson, said in a statement. Unfortunately, 83 people supported by the charity died from cancer last year. “We are continuing to offer bereavement support to their families as they come to terms with their grief.”For families, the value of this support is beyond words. "Having individual support during the last six months for my son has been priceless. He has been able to learn to start to open up more about his feelings to me as his mum and to not be afraid of showing them and communicating his needs,” one parent said.Another parent described how the short break brought so much joy to their child’s life. “It was good for my daughter to talk to someone outside the family and be able to speak about her worries and thoughts. It has helped her deal with her emotions and worries and what she feels inside. She is back to being the happy child we had before cancer made an appearance in our lives.”Over the decade, the lodge has celebrated 280 birthdays, held 7,950 therapeutic workshops and offered 8,925 complementary therapies, according to the charity. The kitchen team has also baked 82,000 pieces of Daisy Lodge shortbread! It may not seem exciting to everyone. But for a family in the middle of treatment, a baking class or a massage can be the first hour in weeks that feels ordinary.The charity is also planning a second lodge, Daisy Lodge Cong, in County Mayo, so it can support more families.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bhopal homemaker Anjita Sabhlok has turned old newspapers and plastic bottles into a way to buy food; her Kachra Cafe initiative says it sent more than 45 tonnes of household waste for recycling in eight months
articles.summary: Old newspapers, empty plastic bottles, cardboard boxes and discarded household items usually end up in a waste bin or are sold to a scrap dealer.
articles.body: Old newspapers, empty plastic bottles, cardboard boxes and discarded household items usually end up in a waste bin or are sold to a scrap dealer. But in Bhopal, these everyday items can help people get a meal, a cup of coffee or other essentials. Homemaker Anjita Sabhlok started Kachra Cafe, an initiative that allows residents to exchange recyclable household waste for food, drinks and everyday products.In just eight months, the initiative has sent more than 45 tonnes of waste for recycling. The idea is to make waste segregation more than an environmental responsibility by giving people a practical reason to do it.According to the official website of Kachra Cafe, Sabhlok launched it through her NGO, Mannat, in collaboration with the Bhopal Municipal Corporation. The initiative aims to encourage residents to separate recyclable waste at home instead of throwing everything away together.The question that led to Kachra CafeSabhlok had been working on environmental awareness and waste management through Mannat for several years. However, she felt that educating people about the importance of waste segregation was not translating into enough action. As she wondered, “We’re educating people, but are we really seeing a change?”This made her think of a different approach. Instead of repeatedly asking people to manage their waste responsibly, she wanted to give them an incentive to do so. That thought eventually became Kachra Cafe. The concept allows residents to bring recyclable materials collected from their homes and exchange them for food and everyday essentials. Each category of waste has a fixed value, making the process simple for customers.How does Kachra Cafe work?The process begins at home. Residents collect recyclable materials such as old newspapers, plastic packets, cardboard, books, clothes and electronic waste and bring them to a Kachra Cafe collection centre. The waste is weighed and its value is calculated according to the material and quantity. Customers receive credits, also known as Kachra Coins or Kachra Currency, which they can redeem for food, beverages and other products.According to the cafe's official website, different materials have different exchange rates. For instance, paper is valued at Rs 15 per kg, books and notebooks at Rs 14 per kg, milk packets at Rs 12 per kg and hard plastic jars at Rs 14 per kg. Soft plastic is valued at Rs 20 per kg, while electronic waste is listed at Rs 50 per kg.The website also lists rates for other materials, including Rs 90 per kg for beverage cans, Rs 120 for aluminium, Rs 30 for iron, Rs 400 for brass and Rs 600 for copper.The collected waste is channelled towards recycling rather than being mixed with regular household garbage. Customers can then use the credits they earn to access food and other products through the initiative's participating outlets.More than 45 tonnes of waste sent for recyclingGetting people to change their everyday waste-disposal habits was not easy initially. Household waste is often treated as something that needs to be thrown away, and convincing residents to collect and separate it requires consistent effort. However, as awareness about the exchange model spread, more people began bringing recyclable materials to the cafe.According to The Better India, Kachra Cafe has sent more than 45 tonnes of waste for recycling in eight months. The initiative has also encouraged residents to learn how to segregate different materials so that they can enter appropriate recycling channels.The cafe's approach gives people a direct benefit for participating in waste management. Instead of depending only on environmental awareness campaigns, it connects recycling with something residents can use in their everyday lives.An idea that could extend beyond BhopalFor Sabhlok, the initiative is not limited to running a cafe in one city. She wants other cities to explore similar models that make waste segregation easier and more rewarding for residents. The larger ambition is to encourage communities to recognise the value of recyclable materials and make responsible waste disposal part of their daily routines.Kachra Cafe's model brings together two everyday concerns: the need to manage household waste responsibly and the need to make food and essential products accessible through a practical exchange.You use AI every day. articles.title: At 35, John Disselkamp quit a Louisville, Kentucky bank to mop floors for $600 a month; his First Class Commercial Cleaning now earns about $10 million a year, with 300 staff
articles.summary: Discover how John Disselkamp left his stable bank job to create First Class Commercial Cleaning, transforming his life and earning $10 million annually with 330 staff across the U.S.
articles.body: In an era when bank jobs are synonymous with financial stability and career success, John Disselkamp chose a unique career path. Instead of pursuing an office job, he abandoned his banking career in pursuit of understanding the commercial cleaning business. This included going back to zero financially and getting into an entirely new line of work.According to a January 24, 2024, Entrepreneur report, Disselkamp gave up his banking job in Louisville at the age of 35. He started as a janitor, earning $600 per month. He later founded First Class Commercial Cleaning in January 2016. The company grew into a business generating about $10 million in annual revenue and employing 300 people. His business started with office cleaning but has expanded to commercial services involving large office buildings and other professional facilities.Leaving a banking career Disselkamp decided to move away from banking not because of a new business opportunity or an already secured financial background. After working for several years in the banking industry, he began to doubt whether he wanted to devote his life to sitting behind a desk. Gradually, his desire to build something of his own grew stronger, prompting him to become an entrepreneur. The business model that interested him in particular was the recurring revenue model through a commercial cleaning contract. The idea of starting a commercial cleaning business came to him from a former customer in the banking industry who had created his own profitable company in the field.This phase was challenging: after quitting his job, Disselkamp moved in with his mother because he had $20,000 in credit card debt and no retirement savings. Later, he got employed in a janitor’s position, making about $600 monthly. This work enabled him to discover what it means to maintain commercial facilities, from choosing cleaning products to dealing with different types of floors and fulfilling the expectations of customers. At first, he lacked practical experience and often consulted people who had done the job before him.A cold call helped to secure the first major contractDisselkamp formally established First Class Commercial Cleaning in January 2016. The venture’s early growth depended on winning back the confidence of commercial clients, who can be cautious about working with a new company. One of the first big chances came as a result of constant attempts to contact local property management firms. He found a contact person on the company’s website and began calling. The calls weren't answered at first, but he kept trying, and the property manager eventually agreed to take his call. The conversation led to a contract to clean an eight-floor building of about 200,000 square feet.Securing the contract was a major milestone for the company. This was an opportunity for the company to establish itself as a reliable cleaning association working with bigger firms. Then, the company started moving from individual cleaning jobs to recurrent contracts for office buildings and other professional places. Eventually, it expanded its services to include commercial floor cleaning, carpet cleaning, window cleaning, day porter services, and post-construction cleaning.Building a business around employees and customer relationshipsThe expansion of the firm has been directly linked to Disselkamp’s focus on relationships and employee engagement within the workplace. Instead of viewing the cleaning process as just another service delivered by completing tasks, he has made efforts towards creating an environment where employees are treated well. He has often reiterated that the success of the company will depend upon the people doing the task, ranging from cleaners to supervisors and management. As stated in the interview with Entrepreneur in January 2024, he stressed the need to know about employees' personal lives to foster an atmosphere of trust in the workforce. This is because a good relationship between employees and management will help provide more consistency in service delivery.The company's financial growth has earned it recognition in the Louisville business community. According to Louisville Business First, First Class Commercial Cleaning generated revenue of $4.89 million in 2022, $9.14 million in 2023, and $10.84 million in 2024. This growth of 121.96% between 2022 and 2024 placed the company seventh on the publication's 2025 Fast 50 list. The business has also expanded beyond its original Louisville market and now provides services in Lexington, Indianapolis, Nashville, and St. Louis. Its expansion reflects the progress made since founder John Disselkamp established the company in January 2016, building it from a small commercial cleaning operation into a business with more than 300 employees nationwide.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fresh lifeline for stalled ₹157.5cr sewerage project; Dec restart likely
articles.summary: Thiruvananthapuram Corporation plans to restart the stalled ₹157.5cr Attukal-Kalady-Ambalathara sewerage project in Dec using 16th Finance Commission funds.
articles.body: T’puram: A fresh lifeline appears to be in sight for the stalled Rs.157.5-crore sewerage project covering Attukal, Kalady and Ambalathara, with the city corporation moving to tap 16th Finance Commission funds and aiming to resume work in the first week of Dec.The corporation council approved the proposal on Saturday, opening a fresh funding route for the project that had come to a halt amid financial constraints. The proposal will now be placed before the district planning committee on Monday as part of the approval process.Corporation secretary Muhammad Shafi said all pending bills related to the project would be paid, including Rs 6 lakh required for obtaining road-cutting permission from the public works department (PWD). He said funding issues that had affected the progress of the project were being addressed.He added that the existing contractor could resume the work once the funding process was completed, and there would be no need to call a fresh tender, potentially avoiding further delays.The project had faced a major setback after the Rs 66.63-crore National Housing Bank (NHB) loan secured for it lapsed. The loan, availed in Sept 2024, lapsed in Feb 2026 after the required work-status report was not communicated to the NHB. The corporation came to know about the lapse only in July, adding to the uncertainty over the project’s funding.The funding crunch subsequently affected payments and the pace of work. The contractor had already mobilised labour and machinery, and around 1km of sewer pipeline work had been completed before the project was stalled. The corporation is now moving to clear pending payments and address other requirements, including the Rs 6 lakh PWD payment, before restarting the work.The two packages are now estimated at Rs166.5 crore and Rs 22 crore.The proposed Dec restart is particularly significant for Attukal ahead of next year’s Attukal Pongala. Timely completion of the pipeline works and restoration of excavated roads will be crucial for traffic movement and access to the temple area when lakhs of devotees converge on the locality.Stay updated with the latest Thiruvananthapuram news.
